title: Propaganda and Misinformation on Facebook and Twitter during the Russian Invasion of Ukraine
screen_reason: Longitudinal platform study (1 January - 24 April 2022) of 19.5M CrowdTangle Facebook posts (2.9 billion interactions) and ~250M tweets matching 40+ multilingual Russia-Ukraine conflict keywords. Reports the share of posts/tweets and of Facebook interactions carrying links to Russian state propaganda outlets and to Iffy Index low-credibility domains, with explicit counts and denominators.

estimates.country: not restricted (multilingual keyword corpus on the Russia-Ukraine war; authors note the data is Western-platform-centric)
estimates.platform: Facebook (public pages and groups via CrowdTangle)
estimates.measure_type: % of conflict-related Facebook posts that shared a link to a Russian state propaganda outlet
estimates.value_raw: 51,269 posts (0.25% of all posts) sharing links to Russian propaganda outlets
estimates.denominator: 19.5 million Facebook posts shared by 1.1 million public pages and groups matching over 40 English, Russian and Ukrainian conflict keywords
estimates.definition: The post contained a link whose domain is on the list of 24 Russian state-affiliated propaganda websites (23 from VoynaSlov plus yandex.ru)
estimates.misinfo_def: "a list of 23 state-affiliated Russian media websites, manually verified by a fluent Russian speaker, which have been flagged for sharing unsubstantiated claims and Russian propaganda about the war"
estimates.source_quote: On Facebook, we identified 51,269 posts (0.25% of all posts) sharing links to Russian propaganda outlets, generating 5,065,983 interactions (0.17% of all interactions)
estimates.page_loc: p. 68, Section 4.1 'Prevalence of misinformation about the conflict'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Distant supervision on the source domain. Russian propaganda list = 23 state-affiliated Russian media sites from the VoynaSlov dataset, manually verified by a fluent Russian speaker, plus yandex.ru. Articles themselves were never verified: 'We did not manually verify the articles published from misinformation sources, but relied on literature supporting the distant-supervision approach'.
estimates.moderator_quote: we queried the /posts/search endpoint weekly, using a set of over 40 keywords (in English, Russian and Ukrainian language) related to the conflict
estimates.notes: State propaganda rather than falsity per se: the list is of outlets flagged for unsubstantiated claims and war propaganda. Denominator is ALL conflict posts, including those with no link at all, so the figure is the share of the conflict conversation, not the share of shared links. Authors call it a lower bound twice over: shortened links (bit.ly etc.) were not resolved, and only news-article links were counted, not claims in text, images or video. CrowdTangle covers only public pages and groups above a follower threshold, not individual users. The paper never reports a combined propaganda+low-credibility share; summing 0.25% and 0.4% would be a cross-category sum barred by R8.

estimates.source_quote: 80,066 posts (0.4% of all posts) sharing links to low-credibility news websites, generating 28,334,900 interactions (0.95% of all interactions)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Iffy Index of Unreliable Sources (600+ domains, built on Media Bias/Fact Check credibility ratings, political leaning explicitly excluded as a criterion). No article-level verification, no reliability statistic.
estimates.moderator_quote: We follow a distant-supervision approach, widely adopted in the literature, to label news articles based on the reliability of the source.
estimates.notes: Disjoint from the Russian propaganda row, not a stricter or broader version of it, so definition_variant=false on both. Same lower-bound caveats (unresolved shortened links, news-article links only). For scale, high-credibility sources (a hand-picked set of 10 reputable outlets) accounted for 0.73% of posts, so unreliable-source posts were roughly comparable in volume to the reputable-source benchmark used here.

estimates.moderator_quote: The resulting dataset contains 19.5M posts, shared by 1.1M unique pages and groups, generating over 2.9 billion interactions (shares, comments, reactions, etc).
estimates.notes: Engagement-weighted counterpart of the 0.25% post-share row: denominator is interactions, not posts, so per the DENOMINATOR-sets-construct rule it is still SHARING (engagement), not EXPOSURE. borderline=true because 'interactions' pools reshares, comments and reactions, which mix amplification with reaction, and a comment may be critical of the content. Propaganda posts got FEWER interactions per post than average (0.17% of interactions from 0.25% of posts).

estimates.source_quote: On Twitter, we identified 567,587 tweets (0.2% of all tweets) sharing links to Russian propaganda outlets, 997,886 tweets sharing links to low-credibility news websites (0.4% of all tweets) and 3,949,774 tweets sharing links to high-credibility news websites (1.6% of all tweets).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same VoynaSlov-derived Russian state outlet list; source-level distant supervision, no article verification.
estimates.moderator_quote: We remark that the streaming endpoint filters tweets that match a defined query in a real-time fashion up to 1% of the global stream. As it can be seen in panel c of Figure 1, we likely hit the rate limit during the weeks following the invasion (February 24, 2022), when the data volume caps at around 4M daily tweets.
estimates.notes: Confidence medium because the Twitter denominator is compromised: the collection hit the streaming API's 1% cap in the weeks after the invasion, so the corpus is a truncated and possibly non-random slice of conflict tweets exactly when volume peaked. Over 70% of the tweets are in English. Same unresolved-shortlink and news-links-only lower-bound caveats.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) NO CONCENTRATION ROW IS POSSIBLE, despite concentration being one of the paper's four research questions. Every concentration statement identifies the group by a raw count, never as a percentage of accounts: 'the top 15 accounts ... generate over 80% of all interactions around links to Russian propaganda and low-credibility information websites' (Facebook), 'the top 15 accounts generate roughly 30% of all retweets linking to low-credibility websites' and 'over 68% of all retweets' for propaganda (Twitter), and the abstract's 'a handful of them accounts for 60-80% of all the reshares and retweets'. The number of accounts sharing each kind of content is never reported, so conc_group_pct cannot be filled and R1 fails. This is the single most consequential omission for the review. 2) Verified-account shares are the same problem: median daily share of interactions from verified accounts is 88.34% (Russian propaganda) and 85.73% (low-credibility) on Facebook, 66.99% and 18.53% on Twitter, but the verified accounts' share of all accounts is never given. 3) Pre/post-invasion median daily proportions are verbatim and could each be a time-sliced row, but the instructions say to collapse time series to one representative point, and the whole-period figures already extracted are that point. For the record, Facebook posts: Russian propaganda 0.62% pre-invasion to 0.15% post; low-credibility 0.22% to 0.42%; high-credibility 0.59% to 0.79%. Facebook interactions: propaganda 0.81% to 0.06%; low-credibility 0.30% to 0.95%; high-credibility 1.24% to 2.20%. Tweets: propaganda 0.52% to 0.16%; low-credibility 0.30% to 0.38%; high-credibility 1.30% to 1.55%. 4) High-credibility shares (Facebook 0.73% of posts and 2.13% of interactions; Twitter 1.6% of tweets) are the reliable-source benchmark, not misinformation, and rest on a hand-picked set of only 10 outlets. 5) Content moderation figures (~10% of Facebook propaganda posts, over 8% of low-credibility posts, ~7% of random posts removed; ~11.9% and over 15% of the corresponding tweets, ~11% of high-credibility tweets; abstract summary '8-15%') measure platform removal, not prevalence. 6) '40% of the comments in the r/Russia subreddit promote Russian mis/disinformation' is cited from Hanley et al., which R8 forbids keeping. 7) Political leaning medians (propaganda spreaders 0.03, low-credibility spreaders 0.20, all users -0.15) are ideology scores, not prevalence. 8) No combined 'any misinformation' share is reported for either platform; the two source lists are disjoint but summing them is barred by R8.

rob.design: Two keyword-matched platform corpora over 1 January - 24 April 2022. Facebook: CrowdTangle /posts/search queried weekly with 40+ English/Russian/Ukrainian conflict keywords, yielding 19.5M posts from 1.1M public pages and groups and 2.9 billion interactions; CrowdTangle covers only public pages and groups above a follower threshold, not individual users, and 42% of posts have no detected language. Twitter: an existing streaming-endpoint dataset (22 February - 24 April) plus historical Search API v2 backfill (1 January - 21 February), ~250M tweets from 15M users, over 70% English; the authors state they likely hit the streaming API's 1% global-stream cap in the weeks after the invasion. Misinformation labelled by distant supervision on the source domain: 23 VoynaSlov Russian state outlets manually verified by a fluent Russian speaker plus yandex.ru, and the 600+ domain Iffy Index built on Media Bias/Fact Check with political leaning excluded. No article-level verification and no inter-coder reliability. Authors flag as limitations: unresolved shortened links, only news-article links counted (no claims in images, video or plain text), no bot accounting, and Western-platform bias that under-covers Russia and Ukraine themselves. Both estimates are explicitly framed as lower bounds. IRB-approved (#UP-21-00005-AM001); post and tweet IDs released.
rob.item6_quote: We referred to the VoynaSlov dataset to obtain a list of 23 state-affiliated Russian media websites, manually verified by a fluent Russian speaker, which have been flagged for sharing unsubstantiated claims and Russian propaganda about the war. ... For what concerns low-credibility news websites, we referred to the Iffy Index of Unreliable Sources, a list of over 600 low-credibility domains based on information provided by the Media Bias/Fact Check website (MBFC, mediabiasfactcheck.com) in which political leaning is not a factor.
rob.item10_quote: On Facebook, we identified 51,269 posts (0.25% of all posts) sharing links to Russian propaganda outlets, generating 5,065,983 interactions (0.17% of all interactions); 80,066 posts (0.4% of all posts) sharing links to low-credibility news websites, generating 28,334,900 interactions (0.95% of all interactions); and 147,841 posts sharing links to high-credibility news websites (0.73% of all posts), generating 63,837,701 interactions (2.13% of all interactions).
